props.title: Punk: Attitude

sections.content: Punk: Attitude stands as Don Letts' definitive documentary on punk's explosive cultural impact. The film brilliantly connects the raw energy of early pioneers like The Velvet Underground (1965) to the full-blown punk explosion with the Ramones and Sex Pistols. What sets this doc apart is how it traces punk's DNA through The Decline of Western Civilization (1981) and shows its evolution beyond just music - capturing the DIY ethic that influenced everything from xeroxed zines to guerrilla filmmaking.

sections.content: The film's genius lies in showing how punk wasn't just about music - it was an attitude that infected film. Directors like Alex Cox captured this spirit in Repo Man (1984) and Sid & Nancy (1986), bringing punk's anarchic energy to cinema. Meanwhile, Downtown 81 (1981/2000) caught the NYC art-punk scene in real time with Jean-Michel Basquiat wandering through a gritty lower Manhattan.

Beyond just documenting shows, punk filmmaking developed its own aesthetic - choppy edits, handheld cameras, and raw production values seen in works like The Blank Generation (1976) and D.O.A. (1980). This DIY approach influenced indie film movements, setting the stage for directors like Jim Jarmusch and his breakthrough Stranger Than Paradise (1984). SUBHEAD: Legacy and Evolution

sections.content: The film shows how punk's influence extended into the 90s and beyond. 1991: The Year Punk Broke (1992) captures Sonic Youth and Nirvana just before grunge exploded. Meanwhile, docs like American Hardcore (2006) and The Other F Word (2011) trace how punk adapted and evolved while keeping its rebellious spirit. Even modern films like Green Room (2015) tap into punk's dangerous energy and outsider perspective.
